title: Do You Need A Chimney Liner? Signs, Types & Cost | Northmark
description: What a chimney liner does, how to tell if yours is cracked or missing, clay vs stainless, and why a new liner fixes many old Toronto chimneys.
h1: Do You Need A Chimney Liner? How To Tell, And What The Options Are
lead: The liner is the part of the chimney you cannot see and the part that keeps heat and gases where they belong. Many Toronto chimneys built before the 1950s have none, and many newer ones have clay liners that have cracked. Here is how to tell which yours is, and what to do about it.

hero.alt: Looking down a chimney flue from the top, inside a Toronto chimney

hero_caption: Looking down the flue: a liner carries the smoke and heat up the chimney and keeps them away from the masonry and the house.

sections.body:
A chimney is a masonry shaft. The liner is the smooth, sealed passage inside it that the smoke and combustion gases actually travel through. It does three jobs: it keeps the heat of the flue gases away from the brick and the wood framing around the chimney; it keeps carbon monoxide from seeping through cracks in the masonry into the house; and it gives the gases a smooth, correctly sized path so the fireplace draws properly.

Without a liner, or with a damaged one, the masonry takes the heat and the acids in the smoke directly. Mortar joints erode from the inside, and a chimney fire — creosote in the flue igniting — can reach the framing.

• Clay tile. Square or rectangular terracotta sections, stacked and mortared, built into the chimney when the house was built. Standard in Toronto houses from roughly the 1920s on. Cheap and durable when intact, but the joints between tiles open up over time, and tiles crack from heat and from water freezing in them.
  • Stainless steel. A flexible or rigid stainless pipe, run down the existing chimney and sealed at top and bottom, usually with insulation around it. This is the standard fix for a cracked clay liner or an unlined chimney, and the standard way to connect a wood stove or insert.
  • Cast-in-place. A cement-like lining poured around a form inside the chimney, creating a new smooth flue. Used when the chimney is unusually shaped or structurally weak; less common.

sections.h2: Signs your liner is damaged or missing
sections.body:
• Pieces of clay tile in the firebox or on the smoke shelf.
  • A chimney built before about 1950 with no visible tile at the top of the flue.
  • Mortar joints on the outside of the chimney that are eroding from the inside out, or a chimney that is warm to the touch on the outside during a fire.
  • A smoky fireplace that never drew well — often a flue that is the wrong size for the fireplace opening.
  • A home inspection, WETT inspection or insurance report that says "flue tiles cracked" or "unlined".

Most of these can only be confirmed with a camera. The free inspection runs a camera the length of the flue and gives you the photos — a crack in a tile at the third floor is not something anyone can see from the fireplace.

sections.h2: Why old Toronto chimneys so often need one
sections.body:
Three reasons come up again and again on the chimneys we inspect. Houses from before the war were often built with no liner at all — bare brick on the inside. Houses from the 1950s to 1980s have clay liners whose joints were mortared with the same mortar as the brick, which the acids in wood smoke eat away. And decades of Toronto freeze-thaw, on a flue with no cap, crack the tiles from the top down.

A stainless liner solves all three at once: it is a continuous, sealed pipe inside the old masonry, and it does not care what the brick around it looks like.

The flue is swept and inspected with the camera. The liner is sized to the appliance — a fireplace, a stove or an insert each need a different diameter — and run down from the top of the chimney, insulated, and connected at the bottom. A new top plate and cap seal it at the crown. On most houses it is a one-day job, done from the roof and the fireplace, with no opening of walls.

What it costs depends on the height of the chimney, the diameter, and whether the flue has offsets. You get the price in writing after the camera inspection, before anything is ordered. See chimney liners.

faq.q: Can I use my fireplace if the liner is cracked?
faq.a: We would not. A cracked liner lets heat and carbon monoxide reach places they should not. Have it camera-inspected first; if the crack is minor, the inspection says so.

faq.q: Does a liner fix a smoky fireplace?
faq.a: Often — a flue that is too large for the fireplace opening draws badly, and a correctly sized liner fixes that. If the problem is a blocked flue, a closed damper or the house being too airtight, a liner will not help, and the inspection tells you which it is.

faq.q: Does my insurance require a liner?
faq.a: Insurers rely on the WETT inspection. If the report finds cracked or missing liner tiles, they will usually ask for it to be corrected before they insure a wood-burning appliance. See WETT inspections.

faq.q: How long does a stainless liner last?
faq.a: A properly sized, insulated stainless liner that is swept yearly should last for decades. Manufacturers typically warrant them for a long time; we tell you the warranty on the one we fit.
